title: Adaptive Localization & Data‑Plane Sharding — Reference Architecture for Private Deploys
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

Summary:
This document describes the "Adaptive Localization & Data‑Plane Sharding" reference architecture for Redwood Private deployments. The design targets enterprise customers who require low-latency inference inside VPCs or on-prem sites while preserving tenant isolation, auditability, and safe upgrade/rollback semantics. It covers the control plane handshake, data‑plane sharding patterns, localization policies, day‑2 operational guidance, upgrade/rollback recommendations, and the customer readiness checklist.

Goals and non‑goals:
- Goals:
  - Provide sub-100–200ms P99 request latency for on‑net (same region or edge) traffic for 2K–10K concurrent requests across tenants.
  - Minimize cross‑region egress and encrypted traffic by localizing model inference and KV caches.
  - Ensure graceful fallback to central model variants with no data leakage across tenants.
  - Allow operator-driven re-sharding and capacity reallocation without tenant-visible downtime.
- Non‑goals:
  - This reference is not an exhaustive hardware procurement guide. See customer-requirements in the Customer Requirements Library for those details.

High‑level architecture (textual diagram)

Control Plane (hybrid):
- Customer VPC / On‑prem operator runs a lightweight Control Plane Proxy (CP‑Proxy) that authenticates with Redwood Control Plane. The CP‑Proxy exposes a local management API for operators and receives signed model manifests and sharding policies.
- Redwood Control Plane provides model catalogs, signed quantization profiles, and rollout policies.

Data Plane (sharded, local-first):
- Each deployment is composed of one or more Shard Pools. A Shard Pool is a set of GPU nodes (or CPU nodes for small models) that serve a set of tenants and model variants.
- Shard Pools are organized by: location (edge/region), compute class (A100/RTX/CPU), and latency tier (hot/warm/cold).
- A Traffic Router (local) implements the localization policy and routes requests to the appropriate Shard Pool; it consults a local KV cache (prefix cache) to accelerate repeated requests.

Adaptive localization flow (short):
1. Ingress request arrives at the local API gateway in the customer VPC.
2. Gateway consults the localization policy (local-first, prefer-hot, or central‑fallback) served by CP‑Proxy.
3. If a compatible model shard exists locally and load allows, route to local shard; else evaluate overflow policies (burst to dedicated reserve, fallback to regional shard, or proxy to Redwood hosted).
4. Route includes tenant identity, model version, token budget; runtime enforces tenant isolation and audit logging.

Key components and responsibilities
- CP‑Proxy: auth, manifest sync, policy distribution, limited control plane telemetry. Owner: Redwood + Customer operator.
- Local Traffic Router: runtime‑level routing, shard selection, per‑tenant rate limiting. Owner: Redwood runtime team.
- Shard Pools: GPU nodes with local KV cache, quantization variant images. Owner: Customer (on‑prem) or Redwood (dedicated).
- Observability Agent: samples traces, token counts, and cache hit ratios for shipback. Owner: Customer (data) + Redwood (control).

SLOs and thresholds (recommended)
- P95 latency (local hot shard): <= 60ms.
- P99 latency (local hot shard): <= 200ms (depends on model and seq length).
- KV cache hit rate target: >= 55% for production prompt sets.
- Model load shedding: begin enforced shedding at 85% GPU utilization per shard.
- Safe rollback window: 30 minutes to detect regressions via smoke evals in new shard.

Configuration table (minimum / recommended)
| Component | Minimum HW (per shard) | Network | Ownership | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Hot shard (small model) | 1x RTX A5000 or equivalent | 25 Gbps L2 | Customer / Redwood | < 512 token batch best-effort |
| Hot shard (large model) | 2x A100 80GB or equivalent | 100 Gbps (RDMA preferred) | Customer / Redwood | Enable quantization profile v2 |
| KV cache node | 32 GB RAM, NVMe | Local L2 | Customer | SSD-backed prefix cache |
| CP‑Proxy | 2 vCPU, 4 GB | Encrypted outbound to Redwood | Customer | Runs as a container or VM |

Localization policy primitives
- local-only: only use locally available shards (used for strict data residency scenarios).
- prefer-local: attempt local, fallback to regional or central if unavailable.
- balance-cost: route to cheaper shard under defined latency budget.
- require-audit: deny fallbacks that circumvent audit logging.

Deployment and rollout procedure (operator checklist)
1. Preflight (customer & Redwood): validate hardware inventory, network egress ACLs, and KMS/HSM endpoints.
2. Install CP‑Proxy and Observability Agent in the VPC.
3. Provision Shard Pools as per capacity plan and tag them with location, compute-class, and latency-tier.
4. Deploy Traffic Router with initial localization policy set to prefer-local and conservative shard assignment.
5. Execute smoke evals: run pre-defined evaluation prompt set (10–20 prompts) against hot shard to verify correctness and latency.
6. Gradual ramp: increase traffic 10% every 15 minutes while monitoring P99 and cache hit rate. Pause and rollback if P99 increases > 30% or cache hit drops > 20%.
7. Full cutover: after 100% traffic is on new shards for at least 2 hours with stable metrics, update manifests and mark shards as active.

Rollback and upgrade safety patterns
- Canary + dual‑path traffic: run new model variant in canary shards and shadow 100% of traffic to it. Only promote if quality parity and latency threshold checks pass.
- Transactional model swap: use shard manifests with two active images (current/new) and an orchestrated handoff where in-flight KV cache snapshots are persisted and rehydrated into the new image.
- For immediate rollback: CP‑Proxy marks new shards as draining, Traffic Router rebalances to prior shards, and control plane revokes the new manifest. Maintain forensic evidence (logs, snapshot IDs) for 7 days.

Day‑2 operations checklist
- Daily: verify CP‑Proxy sync health, shard count, and token throughput per tenant.
- Weekly: run replayed synthetic workload to validate latency tail behavior.
- Monthly: rotate signed model manifests and verify model signing certificates in HSM.
- On anomaly: if P99 exceeds agreed threshold, take the following steps:
  1) Increase shard capacity (temporary burst pool) or move traffic to warm shards.
  2) Enable degraded mode (shorten max tokens, increase sampling temperature controls).
  3) If degradation persists > 15 min, initiate rollback.

Operational runbooks (quick links)
- Shard overflow mitigation: steps to add temporary capacity and reroute traffic.
- KV cache corruption recovery: restore last known good snapshot and warm caches with synthetic prompts.
- Audit evidence retrieval: how to assemble per-tenant request logs, model manifest versions, and KMS key IDs for compliance requests.

Example manifest fragment (YAML)
```yaml
shardPools:
  - id: shardpool-edge-nyc-1
    location: nyc1
    computeClass: a100-80
    latencyTier: hot
    capacity: 8
    models:
      - id: redwood-gptx-3b-q4_0
        signedVersion: "2026-01-23-3"
        quantProfile: v2
    policies:
      localization: prefer-local
      maxConcurrentPerTenant: 50
```

Customer readiness checklist (minimal)
- Network: outbound TLS 443 to Redwood Control Plane IP ranges allowed; BGP/VPN established for remote telemetry if requested.
- KMS/HSM: customer-managed key available for model manifest signing verification and telemetry encryption.
- Hardware: minimum shards as per table; RDMA for large model shards is strongly recommended.
- Compliance: defined evidence retention window (default 30 days) and access controls for logs.

Security and isolation controls
- Tenant encryption boundary: per-tenant encryption at rest for KV cache and model artifacts.
- RBAC: CP‑Proxy enforces operator roles; model manifests require a minimum of two signatures (customer ops + Redwood) for production rollouts.
- Audit: every model swap, shard reallocation, and fallback is logged with manifest ID and operator context.

Known limitations and mitigation
- Cold starts for large models: mitigate by pre-warming replicas during busy windows and using smaller quantized variants for tails.
- Cross‑region fallback latency: label fallback policies with expected egress latencies and use balance-cost to avoid surprises.

Appendix — Example monitoring dashboard widgets
- Shard CPU/GPU utilization (1m / 5m / 1h)
- P95/P99 latency by localization policy and model version
- KV cache hit ratio and eviction rate
- Token throughput per tenant and per shard
- Manifest sync lag and CP‑Proxy health
